analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run universal health insurance program covering every American with no premiums or copays, paid for by new taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have provided health coverage to every US resident through state-run programs funded by new payroll, income, and tobacco taxes, was referred to four House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee health coverage, and most private health insurance with a single public program run by the states under federal standards. Every US resident would be entitled to comprehensive coverage — hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, long-term care — with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copays for most care, and doctors would be barred from billing patients extra. It would be funded by a new tax on employers and the self-employed, a new income tax on individuals, and higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Every US resident would gain comprehensive health coverage with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copays for acute and preventive care, no balance billing, and benefits that move with them between states and jobs. Uninsured people would get full coverage; people with employer insurance would keep coverage regardless of job changes; seniors would gain benefits Medicare lacks, like prescription drugs, dental, and long-term care; the medically underserved would get expanded community clinics and school-based health services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every US resident, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every US citizen, national, and lawful resident alien to comprehensive health benefits under a state health security program, with automatic enrollment starting January 1, 1999.
Prohibits deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments for acute and preventive care, and bars providers from billing patients for covered services, so no one faces surprise medical bills.

Covers hospital care, practitioner services, prescription drugs, dental services, mental health and substance abuse treatment, preventive care, hospice, and a share of home and community-based long-term care.
Supersedes Medicare and Medicaid, meaning seniors would gain coverage for services Medicare does not pay for, and prohibits sale of private insurance that duplicates program benefits.
Mandates grants for primary care in medically underserved areas, school-based health sites, and shifts medical training toward primary care, and sets national maximum prices for prescription drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and the self-employed would pay a new health care payroll tax, individuals a new health care income tax, and tobacco users higher excise taxes. Private health insurers would lose the market for duplicative coverage, drug makers would face board-set maximum prices, and workers' compensation carriers would have to reimburse the state plans. Households with income above the poverty line would pay 20–35% coinsurance on long-term care services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, taxpayers, tobacco users, insurers, drug makers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new taxes on every employer, the self-employed, and individuals to fund the program, replacing existing health spending with a much larger visible tax bill, and raises excise taxes on tobacco products.

Recipients would face 20% coinsurance on home and community-based long-term care and 35% on nursing facility services unless their income is at or near the poverty line, so the plan is not entirely free of out-of-pocket costs.

It bans the sale of private health insurance that duplicates covered services, eliminating the private coverage options roughly 160 million Americans then relied on, and concentrates rate-setting, benefit, and budget power in a single federal board.

States that fail to meet federal standards could be placed in receivership, and providers must accept program payment as full payment, a structure opponents would argue removes choice and flexibility for states, employers, and patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades the entire existing system of premiums, deductibles, copays, and job-locked insurance for universal coverage funded by broad new taxes. For households facing medical bills or uninsurance, the gain is large; the costs are the new taxes, the loss of employer plans and private insurance options, and the risk of a single federal board setting prices and budgets for the whole system.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, then sent to subcommittees, and none of the committees ever held a markup or brought it to the floor before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Jim McDermott introduced the American Health Security Act of 1997 on March 20, 1997, with 24 original cosponsors.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to four committees — Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, and National Security — each 'for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.'
In April 1997 the bill was referred to subcommittees: Human Resources, Health and Environment, and Military Personnel, and DOD comment was requested.
No committee held a markup, no hearings are recorded in the action history, the bill never left committee, and no further action appears before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
By the end, 28 members had cosponsored it: 26 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, private health insurers, pharmaceutical makers, and other parts of the existing health financing system kept their role, and employers avoided the new payroll tax; the roughly 40 million uninsured Americans at the time gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, drug makers, employers, and the status quo

for.name: Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it in the House.

for.name: 26 of 206 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Conyers, Pelosi, Waxman, Frank, and Jackson-Lee.

for.name: J.C. Watts
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican support.

against.name: Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: Received the referral as primary committee and never reported the bill out; it was sent to his Health and Environment Subcommittee in April 1997 and stayed there.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral covering the bill's financing provisions and never acted on it; it went to the Human Resources Subcommittee and saw no further action.

against.name: Dan Burton
against.what_they_did: Received a referral and took no recorded action on the bill.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: The bill would have banned duplicative private health insurance and eliminated the employer-based market; the insurance industry has long opposed single-payer proposals of this kind.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent, with a single Republican joining; committee control rested with the Republican majority, which never scheduled action.

industries.note: The bill would prohibit sale of health insurance duplicating covered services and supersede Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee plans, ending the market private insurers administer today. Their loss was the public's gain in this bill, and the bill died in committee.

The bill requires the federal board to set maximum prices for approved prescription drugs and pays pharmacies accordingly, replacing private negotiating. Patients would pay less at the pharmacy; manufacturers would receive less.
The bill raises excise taxes on tobacco products to help fund the program; the cost falls on tobacco companies' customers and shareholders.

Hospitals would receive global budgets and doctors fee-for-service payment from the program, with guaranteed universal patients and no bad debt or billing overhead, but they must accept program payment as full payment and give up private charges. Provider interests were divided in principle even though the bill never advanced.

Employers would pay a new health care payroll tax but would shed the cost of covering employees directly, since the public plan replaces employer insurance. Whether they came out ahead depended on how much they currently spend on health benefits.
